anomaly_def.Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Unbounded growth of buffer caches, plan caches, work areas, and other heaps drives the database process beyond the host’s safe physical-memory envelope.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space in data, log, and temporary areas falls to zero, triggering allocation failures and write stalls.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate available CPU cycles, creating sustained high run-queue pressure and system-wide latency.

Composite anomaly definition: The database simultaneously overruns memory, storage, and CPU resources, so that each critical resource reaches or exceeds its capacity while the workload is executing.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Administrators observe relentless growth of resident memory alongside escalating swap activity; swap I/O floods the storage layer whose free space is already near exhaustion due to bloated data, logs, and oversized temp segments created by memory spills. At the same time, CPU utilization pins near 100 %, with long OS run queues and frequent context switches. Queries that spill from RAM to temp slow dramatically, increasing statement runtimes, amplifying CPU demand, and generating even more temporary and log files that quickly consume the last gigabytes of disk. As space runs out, data-file extensions, sort operations, and log archiving begin to fail, producing allocation errors, checkpoint stalls, and in clustered systems, node fencing or crash-recovery cycles. Monitoring shows simultaneous alerts for memory pressure, disk-full conditions, and CPU saturation, making single-symptom troubleshooting unreliable.

Causal chain and interaction: Excessive memory allocation pushes the OS into paging; paging traffic inflates I/O, which both consumes CPU (kernel time) and writes swap and temp data to disk, accelerating storage exhaustion. As free space disappears, the database is forced to spill active work sets to ever-shrinking temp areas and to retain unrecycled transaction logs, further intensifying disk usage. The additional I/O wait magnifies CPU demand through context switching and spin-waiting, keeping cores saturated and slowing foreground tasks and maintenance jobs that would normally release memory or reclaim space. The throttled CPU in turn delays memory reclamation threads and background checkpoints, perpetuating high memory residency and swelling on-disk footprints. This feedback loop rapidly degrades throughput and can culminate in out-of-memory kills, disk-full aborts, or complete node failure.

entry.official_description: Could not truncate file %s. OS retuned this error: %s
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with file creation, filesystem access, write durability, log persistence, tablespace management, or storage-capacity boundaries.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect filesystem capacity and permissions, verify persistence paths, review log and data placement, and check whether storage latency or write failures are affecting the engine.
